content: An Hfr cell, also known as an Hfr strain, is a bacterium that contains a conjugative plasmid, often referred to as the F plasmid, integrated into its chromosomal DNA. The term Hfr stands for high frequency recombination, a phenomenon first described by Luca Cavalli-Sforza. Unlike a typical F+ cell, Hfr strains, during conjugation with an F− cell, attempt to transfer their entire chromosomal DNA through the mating bridge, also known as the pilus, to the recipient F− cell. This occurs because the F plasmid has inserted itself into the bacterial chromosome at a specific integration site. The F plasmid's natural tendency to transfer itself during bacterial conjugation results in the transfer of the bacterial genome along with it. This makes Hfr cells particularly valuable for studying gene linkage and recombination. Since the rate of DNA transfer through the pilus is consistent, molecular biologists and geneticists can use Hfr strains, often derived from Escherichia coli, to map bacterial chromosomes and study genetic linkage. A common method employed for this purpose is called interrupted mating. During bacterial conjugation, genetic material is transferred from one bacterium to another via the sex pilus. The formation of sex pili and the ability to donate DNA during conjugation require the presence of an F plasmid. This plasmid contains approximately 25 genes, most of which are essential for the production of the sex pilus. Cells containing the F plasmid are designated as F+ cells, while those lacking it are referred to as F− cells. The F plasmid is classified as an episome, meaning it can integrate into the host bacterium's main chromosome. When the F plasmid integrates into the chromosome, the cell is termed an Hfr cell, signifying its high frequency of recombination. An Hfr cell can transfer F plasmid genes to an F− cell during conjugation. During this process, the F episome may carry along chromosomal DNA from the donor cell. Importantly, the donor cell does not lose any genetic material, as the transferred DNA is simultaneously replicated. However, it is exceedingly rare for the entire chromosome of an Hfr cell to be transferred to the recipient. Homologous recombination occurs when the newly acquired DNA aligns and exchanges with homologous regions of the recipient's chromosome. Despite this, the fragile nature of the mating bridge often results in its breakage, leading to incomplete transfer of genetic material. Consequently, the F− cell typically incorporates only a portion of the Hfr cell's genomic DNA for recombination. There is some debate regarding the exact mechanism of DNA transfer. While the pili are essential for initiating contact between the cells, they do not appear to serve as the direct conduit for DNA exchange. Instead, specific proteins are believed to create a channel between the two bacteria, facilitating the transfer of genetic material.
